Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the need for greater
transparency in our calibrator selection process. We completely agree and have
substantially revised the Methods section to provide a clear, step-by-step
account of the development of the TranScale panel.
To improve clarity, we have restructured this section using a numbered, three-
stage framework: 1. Biomimetic Design and Sequence Selection, 2. Production,
Optimization, and Quality Control, and 3. Final Panel Composition and
Sufficiency. The details of TranScale are as follows:
Our initial design criteria, which included creating biomimetic inverted
sequences, incorporating functional diversity (fusions, isoforms), and targeting
a broad range of physicochemical properties (Stage 1).
The practical challenges encountered during production, specifically the
difficulty in synthesizing very long transcripts (>3,800 nt) with the high purity
required for metrological standards.
Our quality-driven optimization process, where we pragmatically shortened
these problematic transcripts to a maximal length that ensured their analytical
purity and integrity. This crucial step demonstrates our commitment to
metrological quality over adherence to an idealized, but practically unattainable,
design (Stage 2).
The validation of the final 100-transcript panel, confirming that it is more than
sufficient for robust calibration, as supported by our analysis in Supplementary
Figure 9 (Stage 3).
We are confident that this new, highly structured description makes our entire
development process fully transparent and addresses the reviewer's concerns
by clarifying the criteria, the practical optimization steps, and the rationale
behind the final composition of the TranScale panel.
Detailed amendments to the Methods section in the revised manuscript:
The TranScale panel was meticulously developed through a three-stage
process to create a high-fidelity biomimetic standard for RNA sequencing.
1. Biomimetic design and sequence selection
Our design process targeted a panel of approximately 100 transcripts that
collectively mirror the human transcriptome. The selection criteria were
multifaceted:
(i) Biomimetic sequence strategy: To preserve structural characteristics while
eliminating sequence homology, each transcript was designed by inverting a
selected human coding sequence (CDS). This novel strategy maintains native
sequence complexity, such as a GC content similar to the hg38 genome, while
ensuring that TranScale reads do not misalign during bioinformatic analysis.
(ii) Functional diversity: The selected sequences represented a range of
biological features, including wild-type genes, clinically relevant fusion genes,
and alternative splicing isoforms.
(iii) Physicochemical range: The initial design aimed for a broad length
distribution from ~500 nt to over 4,000 nt to cover the majority of the human
mRNA length spectrum.
2. Production, optimization, and quality control
This stage focused on translating the computational design into physical RNA
molecules of the highest metrological quality.
(i) Template generation: The full DNA sequence for each calibrator—
comprising a 5' BamHI site, a T7 promoter, the inverted CDS, a 3' 28 bp poly(A)
tail, a T7 terminator, and a final EcoRI site—was synthesized and cloned into a
pMV vector (BGI Genomics). Following sequence verification (Supplementary
Table 1), recombinant vectors were transformed into E. coli DH5α. Template
DNA for in vitro transcription (IVT) was obtained by BamHI/EcoRI digestion and
purified with the Universal DNA Purification Kit (Tiangen).
(ii) In vitro transcription and pragmatic optimization: IVT was performed using
the T7 High Yield RNA Synthesis Kit (Yeasen). A 20 µL reaction containing 1
µg of template DNA, 10 mM of each NTP, 1× reaction buffer, and 2 µL T7 RNA
Polymerase Mix was incubated at 37°C for 4 hours, followed by DNase I
treatment. At this critical stage, we observed that some of the longer target
transcripts (>3,800 nt) yielded impure products due to premature termination.
Prioritizing analytical validity, we systematically shortened these sequences to
a maximal length that permitted consistent, high-purity synthesis.
(iii) Purification and verification: The resulting full-length RNA was purified using
the MEGAclear Kit (Thermo Fisher), and its concentration was estimated with
a Nanodrop. The integrity and purity of each of the 100 final transcripts were
rigorously verified as a single, sharp peak on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (RNA
3. Final panel composition and sufficiency
The final TranScale panel consists of 100 well-defined, high-purity RNA
transcripts. Despite the necessary length adjustments for quality control, the
panel spans a significant range of lengths (500-3,800 nt). Importantly, the utility
of the panel is not contingent on the detection of all 100 calibrators. Our
operational analyses show that robust calibration models (R² > 0.95) can be
reliably constructed using as few as 20-30 well-distributed calibrators,
confirming the sufficiency of the final panel for its intended application
(Supplementary Fig. 10).
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript “A metrological foundation for absolute transcriptomics using
SI-anchored calibrators” introduces TranScale, a panel of ~100 synthetic
biomimetic RNA spike-ins with assigned SI-traceable concentrations via
isotope dilution mass spectrometry (IDMS). These controls emulate key
features of human transcripts (multi-exon genes, alternative splicing, fusions)
and enable absolute quantification of accompanying RNA-seq libraries.
To demonstrate the approach, the authors conduct a multi-laboratory, multi-
platform, multi-protocol sequencing study (12 batches across two sites using
Illumina and DNBSEQ) and show that TranScale reduces inter-batch variability.
Orthogonal validation using droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) shows good
concordance.
Overall, the methodology is detailed, and the experimental execution, including
IDMS workflows, spike-in design, and calibration procedures, is technically
rigorous. The manuscript is generally well prepared; however, its lengthy,
descriptive and overstated text and large multi-panel figures can sometime
obscure a clear and concise understanding of the technology.
Major Points
1. Conceptual novelty relative to prior controls. The overall framework
using synthetic RNA spike-ins to assess and correct sequencing and
quantification biases remains similar to prior approaches (ERCC, Sequins,
MAQC/SEQC controls). While the use of IDMS to generate SI-traceable
absolute concentrations is a notable advance, its practical significance is
difficult to assess without clear demonstration that SI-anchored
calibration enables new analytical capabilities or biological insights.
2. The manuscript would be strengthened by practical examples showing
how IDMS-based calibration improves performance relative to existing
RNA controls in applied or clinical contexts. For example, to substantiate
the benefits of absolute scaling, analyses such as differential expression
with and without calibration, biomarker detection, clinical diagnostic
cases where absolute scaling reveals insights not achievable with
standard normalization would be valuable. The authors highlight
examples such as the MET/GRB2 ratio and ERBB2 amplification, however
these remain unvalidated and constitute observational hypotheses. The
advantages of TranScale are not demonstrated for any specific diagnostic
application or biological analysis, and it is difficult to.
Response to Major Points 1 & 2: Conceptual Novelty and Practical
Significance
We thank the reviewer for these insightful and closely related points, which
address the core of our study's contribution: the practical significance of SI-
anchored absolute quantification. We agree that the conceptual advance of SI-
traceability must be demonstrated through new analytical capabilities and
validated biological insights. We have performed substantial new experiments
to address this directly.
1). Enabling New Analytical Capabilities:
A key conceptual advance of TranScale is its ability to enable quantification on
an absolute scale and inter-gene comparison, moving beyond the relative
comparisons afforded by prior controls. This new analytical capability allows us
to ask not just "is gene A upregulated?", but "what is the absolute molecular
ratio (stoichiometry) of gene A to gene B?".
2). Demonstrating Practical Significance with a Validated Finding:
As the reviewer requested, we provide a concrete example by focusing on our
observation such as the MET/GRB2 ratio and ERBB2 amplification. We
performed droplet digital PCR (dPCR) to orthogonally validate this finding.
It should be clarified that in the original manuscript, we inferred biological
insights for these four genes (MET, GRB2, ERBB2, GRB7) by estimating their
absolute quantities using TransCale calibration, with data derived from a single
sequencing library of the Quartet D5 sample but not reference dataset, which
led to our erroneous hypothesis regarding the co-amplification of the ERBB2
and GRB7 genes in normal samples. To further strengthen the scientific validity
of these inferences, we evaluated and corrected the reference datasets based
on TransCale while accounting for inter-batch reproducibility. This resulted in
an updated reference dataset for Quartet D5 and D6 with reduced uncertainties
than before. During this update analysis, we found the low basal expression of
the GRB7 gene in normal samples, and was not consistently detectable in the
normal sample Quartet D5, consequently, it was excluded from the reference
dataset and was not included in the absolute quantity validation for the Quartet
D5 and D6 samples. We have performed dPCR experiments to independently
and absolutely quantify the genes MET, GRB2, and ERBB2 in our Quartet
samples in the revised manuscript. As validation of Quartet reference datasets
D5 and D6, the new data shows an excellent concordance (y=x, r2=0.99)
between our TranScale-calibrated RNA-seq and dPCR absolute
measurements (Supplementary Fig. 13b, as follows), supporting our hypothesis
regarding the MET/GRB2 ratio.
In contrast, our analysis of the tumor sample LCA revealed that GRB7 was
stably detectable across batches. This provided supporting evidence for our
biological hypothesis regarding the co-amplification and expression of ERBB2
and GRB7 in tumor samples. Consequently, we performed analysis and dPCR
validation of GRB7 and ERBB2 based on the TransScale-calibrated absolute
quantities for the LCA tumor sample as the supplement. As results, this
validation elevated our original observation to a quantitative finding. By
comparing the expression of ERBB2 and GRB7 in normal (Quartet D5 and D6)
versus tumor sample (LCA), we observed significantly elevated overexpression
levels in the latter (Supplementary Fig. 13a, as follows). Furthermore, dPCR
results showed that the expression levels of ERBB2 and GRB7 in LCA were
nearly equivalent (Supplementary Fig. 13a, as follows), the hypothesis of co-
amplification for these key genes was successfully validated at the
transcriptional level in the tumor sample LCA. This direct, quantitative evidence
is no longer an "observational hypothesis," but a quantitative result supported
by two independent methods.

3). Comparison with Prior Controls:
Furthermore, our new comparative analysis against ERCCs (Supplementary
Fig. 14, as follows) indicates that this level of accuracy was not achieved with
this non-biomimetic approach. The ERCC-calibrated absolute values showed
poor concordance with dPCR (Supplementary Fig. 14e, as follows), which
suggests that combining a biomimetic design with SI-traceability is an important
factor for this new analytical capability.
In summary, by providing a validated example of determining absolute
molecular stoichiometry—a task not reliably achieved in our comparison with a
previous standard—we have now demonstrated the practical significance and
conceptual novelty of our SI-anchored approach. We have also expanded the
Discussion to better highlight potential applications, such as understanding
pathway stoichiometry in cancer.
3. The benchmarking focuses on computational batch-correction
methods (SVA, ComBat), and a fairer, more informative comparison
would include other biomimetic RNA controls (ERCC, Sequins) to
compare corrected versus uncorrected workflows.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this exceptionally insightful and
constructive point. We completely agree that a comparison with other physical
standards is essential for a fairer and more informative assessment. Your
suggestion prompted us to conduct a new analysis that has, in our view,
significantly deepened the conclusions of our study.
Since ERCC remains the most prevalent internal control in the field, it was
chosen for a head-to-head comparison. Additionally, although biomimetic
standards like Sequins have been developed, they share the same fundamental
limitation as ERCC: the absence of SI-traceable value assignment, which
precludes their use as true absolute calibrators. Consequently, we ultimately
selected ERCC as the most representative benchmark to highlight the
paradigm shift enabled by TranScale.
To perform this benchmark, we leveraged data from a large-scale, "real-world"
multi-center study recently published in Nature Communications (Wang, D., et
al., 2024). This landmark study assessed RNA-seq performance across 45
laboratories. From this comprehensive dataset, we selected four representative
laboratory batches that used Quartet samples spiked with ERCC controls to
conduct our analysis. Using a well-defined subset from such a peer-reviewed
public dataset provides a robust and unbiased foundation for our evaluation.
The complete analysis of this data is now presented in a new Supplementary
Figure 14. The results were highly informative. When we attempted to use the
ERCC data from this real-world benchmark for absolute abundance calibration,
we observed several unexpected outcomes, including a decrease in biological
signal (SNR) (Supplementary Fig. 14b-c, as follows), an increase in inter-batch
data variability (CV) (Supplementary Fig. 14d, as follows), and the derived
absolute copy numbers showed poor concordance with orthogonal dPCR
measurements (Supplementary Fig. 14e, as follows).
Furthermore, after performing potential absolute quantification calibration via
ERCC, we calculated the inter-sample gene expression ratios (M8/D6) and
used the published Quartet reference dataset13 as the "gold standard" for
external validation. As shown in the Supplementary Table 21, among the genes
detected across the four laboratories, 7,300, 8,040, 6,775, and 9,152 genes
overlapped with those covered by the M8/D6 reference dataset. However, less
than 6% of these genes matched the reference dataset after the potential
calibration by ERCC. These results consistently demonstrate that ERCC spike-
ins fail to achieve absolute quantification calibration for transcriptomic gene
expression in the same manner as TranScale.
We have now incorporated a concise discussion of these findings in our
manuscript. We hypothesize that these results, observed in a large-scale, real-
world setting, stem from the non-biomimetic nature of ERCCs. This provides
strong empirical evidence that a calibrator's design is a critical consideration for
its intended application.
We are truly grateful for your guidance. By pushing us to perform this
comparison, you have enabled us to anchor our findings in a major, community-
wide benchmark study, which we believe makes our conclusions about the
importance of biomimicry much more powerful and generalizable.

Amendments to the Discussions section in the revised manuscript:
This principle of biomimicry is shared by other standards like Sequins12
which were designed with exon-intron structures. However, effective absolute
quantification requires a second, equally important attribute: SI-traceable
certified values. Sequins are provided with defined relative ratios, making them
excellent tools for validating a workflow’s ability to measure fold-changes, but
they are not designed to provide the absolute concentration anchor needed to
build a true calibration curve from sequencing signal to molecular count30, 31.
TranScale is thus developed to address both requirements. It combines a
biomimetic design for representative behavior—a feature empirically shown to
be critical through our ERCC comparison—with the metrological foundation for
true absolute scaling. While no synthetic standard can perfectly replicate all
endogenous transcripts, our results indicate this dual-principled approach
provides a practical and robust solution for absolute transcriptomics.
4. The IDMS workflows and statistical analyses are complex, requiring
specialized equipment and expertise, and use statistical approaches that
are complex, which would be difficult for adoption. To support broader
adoption, a simplified description of the statistics and analytical workflow
would be helpful to support adoption.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding the
complexity and accessibility of our method. We agree that this is a crucial point
for broader adoption. To address this, we have substantially revised our
Discussion to present a clearer framework for understanding the application of
TranScale.
In the revised paragraph, we now frame our method as a tiered approach,
distinguishing the roles of the producer, validator, and end-user:
Metrological Characterization (Producer's Role): We clarify that the complex
IDMS and statistical workflows are confined to the foundational, one-time
characterization of the TranScale reference material, a task performed by a
national metrology institute or a certified producer.
Routine Application (End-User's Role): We emphasize that for the end-user,
the process is designed to be straightforward. We now directly reference our
operational guide in Supplementary Figure 9b (upper panel) to illustrate that the
user-facing workflow involves simple spike-in and a standard linear calibration.
Workflow Validation (Validator's Role): We integrate this with our discussion of
the dual-metric framework, presenting it as a tool for an initial, rigorous
validation of a lab's entire workflow (Supplementary Figure 9b, lower panel),
which is distinct from routine, single-mix use.
By structuring the discussion around this tiered framework, we believe we have
effectively addressed the reviewer's concern about the barrier to adoption. The
revised text now clearly demonstrates that while TranScale is built upon a
complex metrological foundation, its application in a typical research laboratory
is practical, scalable, and accessible.
